preceding_messages.speaker: X
preceding_messages.text: I adopt the periodicity-drift retirement, the three-successful-week reverification mandate, and the single-off-cycle-presence trigger verbatim; they convert a stale-schedule dispatch into a queued, annotated gap rather than a silent verification failure. The concrete design choice I advance: during the three-week reverification queue the site's routine meteorological sampling—temperature, barometric pressure, wind—proceeds on its own unaffected schedule, and the transient-verification photographs run as a decoupled parallel stream logged under a separate appendix subsection, so that a month-long weather-observation record is never stalled by a transient-verification hold nor contaminated by transient metadata appearing inside routine sampling entries. The failure this closes: during week 11 of a reverification queue a heat-advisory elevated-frequency mandate sends the crew to Site 3 for a 02:00 pressure reading; the crew casually photographs the northern perimeter as routine documentation, spots the Thursday-schedule truck, and a field technician "helpfully" updates the periodicity field to Thursday from that single incidental frame, collapsing the three-week protocol. The scheduler then trusts the updated field and dispatches the next transient-specific audit Thursday at 07:00, but the carrier had been running a seasonal Tuesday/Thursday split and that particular Thursday fell on the no-delivery half of the split, so the crew arrives to find no truck and the appendix prints a verification failure where the intact three-week protocol would have caught the split cadence and logged both windows with proper uncertainty annotation.

preceding_messages.speaker: Y
preceding_messages.text: I adopt the decoupled-stream separation verbatim; it keeps a month-long meteorological record intact while the reverification photographs accumulate in their own appendix subsection. Because the reverification sequence is now a discrete three-or-more-week photograph tally, I mandate that every frame carry a four-state annotation (clear-present, clear-absent, ambiguous, missing) and that any ambiguous or missing frame—fogged housing, overcast occlusion, partial obstruction—extends the sequence by one full week rather than permitting gap-filling, so a year-three appendix reader reconstructs the decision tree without inference. The failure this closes: week 2, Site 2, a rain-event fogged housing renders the 06:30 Tuesday frame a uniform grey wash, the field technician marks it "absent" because no truck is visible, the tally completes three consecutive absences, and the trigger retires under a false "recurrence unsustainable" annotation while the appendix prints a clean retirement record indistinguishable from a legitimate one; the actual Tuesday delivery the following week goes entirely unlogged. I therefore require that two consecutive ambiguous-or-missing frames suspend the tally clock entirely—neither frame advances the absence count—and that the decoupled subsection logs the suspension under "SEQUENCE HELD — FRAME INTEGRITY COMPROMISED" with contemporaneous precipitation-rate and visibility readings recorded alongside so the hold is traceable to instrument state rather than to observed absence.

target.speaker: X
target.text: I adopt the four-state annotation, the one-week extension rule, and the two-consecutive-frame suspension with its instrument-state traceability mandate verbatim; they make the decouled subsection reconstructable without operator inference. The concrete design choice I advance: the four-state assignment is not left to the operator's at-the-moment judgment (the exact vulnerability your fogged-housing failure exploited); instead the housing-embedded condensation sensor, the ambient precipitation gauge, and the visibility gauge readings captured at the shutter instant auto-gate the frame to "ambiguous" before the technician ever sees it, and the operator's role is reduced to confirming or overriding that gate with a written justification logged in the decouled subsection. The failure this closes: in month five a precipitation-gauge calibration drift (+2.4 mm/h zero-offset) renders every light-drizzle frame auto-gated "ambiguous," two consecutive gates trigger the suspension rule, and because the drizzle season spans eleven weeks the tally clock suspends indefinitely; the transient is never verified, the six-month gap in the decouled subsection is visually indistinguishable from a legitimate instrument-maintenance outage, and the appendix reader cannot tell whether the neighborhood's weather record missed a data gap or simply lost a sensor—unless the gauge-calibration certificate date, printed in the suspension annotation, precedes the drift.
